catalog_quote: 1.3 Stress. Word stress in Ifira-Mele falls regularly on the antepenultimate vowel, with long vowels treated as two vowels for the purpose of stress assignment. A normal utterance must contain at least three vowels. Speakers will not cite nouns and verbs with just two vowels (including many of the most common words in the language) in isolation, but always with an article, verb prefix or other affix attached.

new_statements.quote: p. 5, 1.6 Stress: "As both Biggs and Capell have observed, stress is consistently on the antepenultimate vowel. Correct stress placement requires counting long vowels as two, as generally in Polynesian languages: /arétuu/ "tomorrow", /tafúraa/ "whale", vs. /átolu/ "egg", /táfuna/ "light oven". The domain of stress placement includes articles, verbal particles, and the locative preposition: /té+ara/ "the road", /á+namu/ "the mosquitoes", /eé+fano/ "goes", /kuú+goro/ "has sung", /í+tai/ "at the shore"." p. 19: "Mele-Fila is also unique among Polynesian languages in having consistent antepenultimate stress. It may be that this, too, is a result of Efate influence."

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog record (Clark 2002 sec. 1.3 / Clark 1998 p. x: regular antepenultimate-vowel stress, long vowels count as two; weight-sensitive with a fixed default). Adds: the explicit statement of the stress domain (articles, verbal particles, locative preposition are inside it), the rule ordering with gliding and vowel deletion, the attribution of the same observation to Biggs (1975) and Capell (1942), and the typological remark that Mele-Fila is unique among Polynesian languages in consistent antepenultimate stress, possibly through Efate (Nguna) contact. It contradicts the Wikipedia 'second-to-last syllable' line already noted in the catalog bundle as disagreeing with the prima…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls consistently on the antepenultimate vowel (mora), with a long vowel counted as two vowels; so in syllable terms the penult when the final or penult syllable has a long vowel, otherwise the antepenult. The stress domain is the phonological word including proclitic articles, verbal (tense/aspect) particles and the locative preposition, which therefore carry the stress before two-vowel stems (té+ara, eé+fano, í+tai). Clark also notes (p. 3, sec. 1.4) that the 'quite regular antepenultimate stress rule' is ordered before the u-gliding rule, and (pp. 5-6, sec. 1.7-1.8) that the particles are stressed before bivocalic morphemes and otherwise unstressed, shortened and deleted (Stress Placement > Particle Shortening > Initial Vowel Deletion).
new_statements.exceptions: none stated for stress placement ('consistently'); the rule interacts with a synchronic initial-vowel deletion that removes unstressed particles (á fare 'the houses' vs pókasi 'the pigs' < a+pokasi). Statements apply mainly to the Mele dialect (fieldwork at Mele village, Dec 1974-Jan 1975).
new_statements.identity_note: Clark 1975's statements 'apply mainly to the Mele dialect' (Mele village, Efate; dialect notes in his sec. 3.1); the p. 19 comparative remark is about Mele-Fila as a whole. Capell 1942, per Clark 1975 p. 1, was based on a young Fila (Ifira Island) man at school in Fiji, so it describes the Fila dialect. Both are the same language, glottocode mele1250.

new_statements.quote: Accent is of some importance, and many enclitics and combinations of grammatical elements affect the accent. [p. 155] Thus the demonstrative ra, “that there” brings the accent forward: tángata, man, but tangatá-ra, that man. Another is the verbal particle e used before numerals: it bears the accent and is lengthened. So e rua, two, is pronounced ērua. [...] Some verbal particles practically combine with the verb and carry the accent back on to themselves: u tuánge tangatá ra kô fa, I told that man to go. The result is therefore something a sentence-accent rather than a strictly word-accent [...] té po, the night; té rea, the sun.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Ifira-Mele / Mele has an empty rule and no existing statements, so Capell adds placement information rather than confirming a recorded one. His examples and his clitic-group domain are consistent with the antepenultimate-vowel rule (long vowels count two; articles, verbal particles and the locative preposition inside the domain) that Clark 1975 'Mele Notes' sec. 1.6 p. 5 states and that Clark explicitly attributes to Capell as well ('As both Biggs and Capell have observed, stress is consistently on the antepenultimate vowel', held by the project from the earlier reading:). Capell describes the Fila (Ifira) dialect; Clark mainly Mele.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Capell does not state a syllable-counting rule in words; he says accent matters and that clitics shift it: an enclitic (demonstrative ra, na) pulls the accent one step rightward (tángata -> tangatá-ra; mārá na), and proclitic particles (article te, numeral particle e, some verbal particles) take the accent onto themselves before short words (té po, té rea, ē-rua, ró-mai), so that the accent behaves as a 'sentence-accent rather than a strictly word-accent'. His accent-marked examples place the accent on the antepenultimate vowel of the word-plus-clitics group (tángata, tangatá-ra, ru-tángata, ró-mai, ē-rua, té po, té rea, mārá na), i.e. a right-edge-counted fixed antepenultimate accent over the clitic group; two surface forms (u tuánge, kitjóna < kite sona) look penultimate. He adds that vowel length and accent are independent (māra keeps its long first vowel when na moves the accent).
new_statements.exceptions: Accent placement is computed over the clitic group, not the lexical word: enclitics ra/na move it rightward, proclitics te/e/ru and some verbal particles can bear it; e before numerals is accented and lengthened (ērua); vowel length is not tied to accent. No lexical exceptions listed.
new_statements.identity_note: Capell 1942 describes the Fila (Ifira islet, Vila harbour) dialect, from a single young Fila speaker interviewed in English at Ndavuilevu, Fiji; he treats Fila and Mele as one language ('Fila-Mele') and contrasts it with Mae (Emae). Clark 1975, the other source held by the project, is mainly the Mele dialect.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: both deciding quotations are present verbatim at the stated places in copies we hold (Clark 2002 p. 682 sec. 1.3 in the scanned text of The Oceanic Languages; Clark 1998 PL C-149 p. x). Deciding source: a 2002 grammar sketch plus a 1998 dictionary introduction, both by Ross Clark, the only linguist to have done sustained fieldwork on Mele; Glottolog lists no grammar, phonology monograph, dissertation or instrumental study for mele1250, and Clark himself says no comprehensive description exists. The classification (antepenultimate vowel/mora, long vowels count double -> weight-sensitive right-edge, CVV heavy) follows directly from the quoted rule.
